TB patient Andrew Speaker set off an international health scare when he traveled to Europe for his wedding in May. When the infected portion of the lung was cut out, it was placed inside a bag while still inside the attorney's chest cavity and the bag was sealed inside a tube before being removed. The main reason for sealing the infected tissue was to prevent it from re-infecting Speaker as it was removed, Gupta said after the operation. Doctors also wanted to make sure they didn't "release any of that tuberculosis bacteria into the operating room, into the rest of the hospital," Gupta said before the surgery on CNN's "American Morning." Watch Andrew Speaker discuss his reasons for having surgery with CNN's Dr. Sanjay Gupta » . Doctors said the operation went well and there was not much bleeding, Gupta said. The portion of the lung that was removed showed the effects of the disease, Gupta said. "A regular lung is very pink with a smooth, glistening surface," he said. "This had a lot of bumps on it, and the areas that were diseased were very dark with white nodules." Speaker will most likely recover at the University of Colorado Hospital for another couple of days, and will return to National Jewish Medical and Research Center in Denver to finish his antibiotic course. He will still have to continue taking the medications prescribed by his doctors to fight the tuberculosis until cultures taken from him are negative for tuberculosis bacteria for eight weeks. At that point, he will be considered non-infectious, but he will still be monitored by health care professionals. Speaker said it was his decision to have the surgery, which is just one of his treatment options. Speaker was originally found to have an extremely drug resistant strain (XDR-TB) of the respiratory disease earlier this year, but on July 3 doctors said he had multi-drug resistant tuberculosis (MDR-TB), which is treatable with less toxic drugs. Speaker and his fiancee had gone to Europe on May 12 for their wedding in Greece, despite warnings from the Fulton County Health Department in Georgia that he should not fly because he risked infecting fellow passengers. Since then, eight people who shared a flight with Speaker have filed a lawsuit against him, seeking $1.3 million in damages. Rosalind Yee -- an attorney for the plaintiffs who said her clients include a ninth person related to one of the passengers but who was not on the flight -- said all eight passengers have undergone TB tests since they returned home. One of them, a 72-year-old man, tested positive for TB on a skin test, though it was not clear that Speaker was the source. The man's X-rays were normal, she said, and he is awaiting results of further tests. In the past year, there have been about 124 cases of MDR-TB in the United States. Speaker made headlines two years ago when health officials revealed he had traveled to Europe and back for his wedding despite being diagnosed with what was initially believed to be extensively drug-resistant tuberculosis, or XDR-TB — one of the most dangerous forms of the disease. The case triggered a global manhunt of sorts, with the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention issuing its first involuntary quarantine order in nearly 50 years to force Speaker into isolation upon his return to the United States.

Subsequent testing revealed Speaker actually had a less severe, though still serious, form of the disease known as multidrug-resistant tuberculosis, or MDR-TB.

CNN's chief medical correspondent, Dr. Sanjay Gupta, has followed Speaker's case closely since it first broke and was granted access to observe aspects of the patient's ongoing treatment. Gupta reported that despite aggressive antibiotic therapy over the past two years, portions of Speaker's lung sustained damage from the infection, necessitating surgical intervention.

"What we're seeing here is really the long tail of this disease," Gupta said. "Even after the infectious component is addressed, patients like Andrew can be left with structural damage to the lung tissue itself. Surgery becomes necessary to remove that damaged tissue, both to improve lung function and to eliminate any reservoir where bacteria might persist."

Gupta noted that Speaker has remained largely out of the public eye since the scandal, focusing on his treatment regimen, which has included months of powerful antibiotics known to carry significant side effects.

"Andrew has been through an incredibly grueling course of treatment," Gupta said. "The drugs used to treat drug-resistant TB are harsher, less effective, and must be taken for a much longer duration than standard TB treatment — often 18 months to two years, sometimes longer."

Doctors familiar with the case say the surgery is not uncommon in patients with Speaker's history, particularly when scarring or persistent cavitary lesions remain in the lung despite drug therapy.

Speaker previously sued the CDC and a Fulton County lab, alleging his medical information was mishandled, contributing to the public disclosure of his diagnosis. He has maintained that he was told by doctors he was not contagious at the time of his travel.

CNN has reached out to Speaker's legal representatives for comment on his current condition and prognosis following the surgery. This is a developing story and will be updated as more information becomes available.

*This report includes medical observations from CNN Chief Medical Correspondent Dr. Sanjay Gupta.*

In the summer of 2007, an Atlanta lawyer named Andrew Speaker became the center of an international health scare that raised serious questions about global disease surveillance, individual rights, and the challenges of containing infectious diseases in an age of easy international travel.

## The Diagnosis and the Decision to Travel

Speaker was diagnosed with tuberculosis shortly before his scheduled wedding in Greece. Initial tests suggested he had a drug-resistant strain of the disease, though the full extent of the resistance was not immediately clear to health officials. Despite being aware of his diagnosis, Speaker proceeded with his travel plans, flying to Europe for his wedding and honeymoon.

The situation escalated dramatically when further testing revealed that Speaker was infected with extensively drug-resistant tuberculosis (XDR-TB), one of the most dangerous forms of the disease. XDR-TB is resistant to multiple first and second-line antibiotics, making it extremely difficult to treat and significantly more likely to be fatal than ordinary tuberculosis.

## The International Response

Once health officials understood the severity of Speaker's condition, an international manhunt of sorts ensued. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) took the unprecedented step of issuing a federal isolation order—the first such order issued by the U.S. government in over 40 years. Speaker was placed on a no-fly list, and officials worked to trace his movements across multiple countries to identify passengers who may have been exposed during his flights.

The case sparked panic among fellow passengers and prompted health authorities in several countries to attempt contact tracing efforts, reaching out to travelers who had been on the same flights as Speaker to advise them on testing and potential symptoms to watch for.

Speaker eventually made his way back to the United States, reportedly crossing the border from Canada, which raised additional questions about border security and the enforcement of travel restrictions for individuals with dangerous infectious diseases.

## Treatment and Recovery

Upon his return to the U.S., Speaker was taken into custody by federal health authorities and transported to National Jewish Health in Denver, Colorado, a hospital renowned for its expertise in treating respiratory diseases, including drug-resistant tuberculosis.

Medical teams at the facility began an intensive treatment regimen. Given the drug-resistant nature of his infection, Speaker's treatment options were limited compared to those available for ordinary TB. Doctors ultimately determined that surgical intervention would be necessary as part of his treatment plan.

Speaker underwent surgery to remove a portion of his infected lung tissue—a procedure sometimes necessary in cases of drug-resistant TB when medication alone cannot adequately address the infection. This surgical approach, combined with a carefully managed course of antibiotics, formed the core of his treatment strategy.

Following the surgery and continued treatment, Speaker's condition improved significantly. Medical tests eventually showed that he was no longer contagious, and he was released from the strict isolation that had confined him during the height of the health scare.

## Broader Implications

The Speaker case highlighted several critical issues in global health security:

**Communication Gaps**: The incident revealed significant communication failures between local health departments, the CDC, and international health authorities. Questions arose about whether Speaker was properly informed of the severity of his condition and the restrictions that should have applied to his travel.

**Legal and Ethical Questions**: The case sparked debate about individual liberty versus public health concerns. Should individuals with dangerous communicable diseases be legally prevented from traveling? What obligations do patients have when diagnosed with contagious, potentially fatal illnesses?

**International Coordination**: The difficulty in tracking Speaker's movements and notifying potentially exposed passengers across different countries exposed gaps in international health surveillance systems and the mechanisms for rapid information sharing between nations.

**Border Security**: Speaker's ability to cross back into the United States despite being on a no-fly list and subject to a federal isolation order raised concerns about the enforcement of health-related travel restrictions at border crossings.

## Conclusion

The Andrew Speaker case ultimately ended without any confirmed transmissions of XDR-TB to fellow passengers, according to follow-up testing of those who could be traced and tested. However, the incident served as a wake-up call for public health officials worldwide, prompting reviews of protocols for handling patients with dangerous drug-resistant infections and highlighting the need for improved international coordination in an era where diseases can cross borders as easily as the people who carry them.

The case remains a significant reference point in discussions of public health policy, individual rights, and the ongoing challenge of balancing personal freedom with collective safety in the face of infectious disease threats.
